2.8.5 CLASSIFICATION SYSTEM Classification is defined as the system of grouping the organisms according to their resemblance or differences in characteristics. Organisms have been classified from different points of view at different times. The various types of classification are described below: a. Artificial system: It is based on one or a few easily observed characters (like habit, habitat, size, etc.) rather than on natural or evolutionary relationships. It is easier and quicker method of classification of organisms in the field. For example, the grouping of plants into herbs, shrubs and trees. There are many drawbacks in this system such as lack of detail information, heterogeneous grouping of organisms, separation of closely related organisms etc. Example: Linnaeus Classification.

b. Natural system: It is based on large number of characters and utilizes all the information available at the time. This system of classification gives us a true idea about natural relationship existing among the organisms. This system of classification avoids the heterogeneous grouping of organisms. Example: Bentham and Hooker’s classification system.

c. Phylogenetic system: It is based on detailed characters of organisms as well as proper phylogenetic and evolutionary characters. It enables to determine the ancestors of any taxon. However, it seems a bit difficult to classify perfectly on the basis of evolutionary tendencies due to imperfection of fossil records. So, at present the organisms are classified partly according to natural and partly according to phylogenetic basis. E.g. Engler and Prantl’s system of classification.
To describe a flowering plant, various morphological features are used. The features should be
brief, with semi technical terms and presented in a proper sequence. The families are described
starting with its habit and habitat, morphological characters of root, stem, leaf and flower. Then
after, a floral diagram and a floral formula are presented.
